senses: Capable of being instructed; receptive to instruction or education.
ety: From instruct + -able.
examples: Yet another division placed persons depending on their ability to receive teachings: those who need only condensed teaching, those who need expanded teaching, and those who are barely instructable.

senses: Marked or covered with large, irregular spots.
ety: From an alteration (due to splotch) of Middle English splotty, equivalent to splotch + -y. * IPA⁽ᵏᵉʸ⁾: /ˈsplɒ.tʃi/ * Audio (Southern England): (file) * Rhymes: -ɒtʃi

senses: Remaining or persisting especially after an electrical or magnetic influence is removed.
ety: From Latin remanens, present participle of remaneō (“to remain”).

senses: To secrete or produce milk.
ety: Borrowed from Latin lactātus, perfect passive participle of lactō (“to suckle, give suck, contain milk”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lac (“milk”), cognate to Ancient Greek γάλα (gála, “milk”).

senses: One who is looked at.
ety: From look + -ee.

senses: Someone who delivers coal.
Someone who sells coal.
A coal miner (as distinguished from other type of miners).
ety: From coal + -man.

senses: A person who studies or practises genealogy; an expert in genealogy.
ety: From genealogy + -ist.

senses: An artist who paints landscapes.
A landscape gardener.
ety: From landscape + -ist.

senses: A tripod or stand for a cask, a haystack, etc.
ety: From Middle English brandreth, from Old English brandrād, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *brandaraidō.
examples: Paid for working 5 stone of iron of the old “brandreth” at 2d. 10d.

senses: Visual inspection of the ureter by means of a ureteroscope.
ety: From ureter + -scopy.
examples: In accordance, the five completely normal ureteroscopies in our study were performed in patients with small filling defects on CTU.

senses: A vacant lot where children play.
ety: From sand + lot.
examples: Many great players started out playing sandlot baseball.

senses: A fudge confection or cookie.
ety: From fudge + -ie. The tourists were so named because their main reason to travel was for the famous fudge. As a food name, possibly influenced by brownie or cookie.
examples: Those who find their way through the tunnels underneath the Boardwalk to the beach are met by hawkers selling fudgies.
Mary’s Fudgies / These bars are delicious frozen, when they become like chewy toffees.
This Canadian company offers an assortment that is “simple but tasty” (like the Pecan Caramel), “old-fashioned” (the Rum and Butter Fudgie), and “totally delicious” (the Strawberry Rosa).

senses: The generation of methane by anaerobic bacteria.
ety: From methane + -o- + -genesis.

senses: An analytic instrument that estimates the concentration of a substance in a sample by measuring its color against the solution's complementary color.
ety: From color + -meter. Compare Latin color, colōris.

senses: Someone or something that greases (applies grease).
ety: From grease + -er. Applied to mechanics because they frequently become greasy during the course of their work. Applied to toughs because they frequently greased their hair, and, like greaseball, to Italians for the same reason. Applied to Mexicans because, at the time the phrase originated, they commonly worked greasing the axles of carts.

senses: The wood pigeon, Columba palumbus.
ety: From Middle English quiste, quyste, quyshte, variants of Middle English couschot, cowschote, cowscott, from Old English cūsċeote (“wood pigeon, ringdove”). Doublet of cushat.

senses: A South Asian dish of seasoned mashed vegetables or eggs.
ety: From Hindi भरता (bhartā) / भुरता (bhurtā) (cf. Bengali ভর্তা (bhorta)).
examples: I love her chicken curry, chicken bharta, chicken kasha.

senses: A hard-shelled fruit from a plant in Lagenaria or Cucurbita.
The dried and hardened shell of such fruit, made into a drinking vessel, bowl, spoon, or other objects designed for use or decoration.
Loaded dice.
ety: From Middle English gourde, from Anglo-Norman gurde, gourde, from Latin cucurbita. Doublet of cucurbit.

senses: One who pumps something.
A fire engine with a water tank and pump.
ety: From pump + -er.

senses: A sedimentary rock whose composition is intermediate in grain size between the coarser sandstone and the finer mudstone.
ety: From silt + stone.

senses: A sedan-type (saloon-type) car.
ety: Borrowed from French berline.

senses: A thing, condition, or other matter which is exceptional.
the condition of requiring special schooling for reasons of intellectual giftedness or physical or mental disability
ety: From exceptional + -ity.
examples: We are fain to ask what is to become of Shakespeare and a host of others, who, with equal originality of thought, have avoided those vagrant exceptionalities of humour.

senses: A Germanic unit of currency used between the 15th and 19th centuries.
ety: From German Taler, (older) Thaler. Doublet of dollar and tolar.

senses: Obscene; filthy; unchaste.
Sexual in nature and usually meant to be humorous but considered rude; ribald.
ety: From bawd + -y.

senses: Similar to the nature of a beast; contrary to the nature and dignity of human beings.
Abominable; very unpleasant; hideous.
ety: From Middle English bestely, bestly, equivalent to beast + -ly. Compare West Frisian bistachtich (“beastly”), Dutch beestachtig (“beastly”), German biestig (“beastly”).

senses: A rough woolen cloth; caddice.
A kind of worsted lace or ribbon.
ety: From Middle French cadis, from Old French cadaz, from Old Occitan, from Old Catalan cadirs, cadins.

senses: A traditional Japanese military helmet, especially worn by samurai.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 兜 or 冑 (かぶと, kabuto).

senses: Saussurea costus, a composite growing on the Himalayas in the vicinity of Kashmir, or its root.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin costus, from Ancient Greek κόστος (kóstos), from Sanskrit कुष्ठ (kuṣṭha).

senses: Of or belonging to a king or kings; exercised by a king.
Characteristic of kings, majestic, regal; as befits a king, in the manner of a king.
ety: From Middle English kyngly, from Old English *cyninglīċ (“kingly, royal”), equivalent to king + -ly. Cognate with Dutch koninklijk (“kingly, royal”), German königlich (“kingly”), Swedish kunglig (“kingly”). Compare also Old English cynelīċ (“kingly, royal, public”).
examples: Leave kingly backs to cope with kingly cares; They have their weight to carry, subjects theirs;
Tho' trouble-tried, and torture-torn, / The kingliest Kings are crown'd with thorn.
As for Bradly, he reclined in kingly ease, smoking austerely, and ejecting a grunt at intervals into her narrative, confessing an interest in it.

senses: The process by which cells from beneath the skin are converted to hair and nails (made of keratin).
ety: From keratin + -ization.

senses: Divided into zones.
Related to, associated with, or similar to zones.
roughly longitudinal (east to west, or west to east)
ety: First attested 1865–70, from zone + -al.

senses: The study of the relationship between the nervous system and the immune system, especially with regard to autoimmune conditions
ety: From neuro- + immunology.

senses: Capable of being explored.
ety: From explore + -able.

senses: One who flosses the teeth.
A tool used for flossing the teeth, consisting of a disposable pick with floss stretched across it.
An angler who uses a weighted hook that pierces the fish's mouth from the outside.
ety: From floss + -er.

senses: Something which covers; a covering or coating.
ety: Also in late Middle English, borrowed from Latin tegumentum (“a cover”), from tegere (“to cover, clothe”, verb) + -mentum (suffix forming nouns). Compare integument.

senses: Having or furnished with seams.
ety: From Middle English semed, equivalent to seam + -ed.
examples: Over those seamed cheeks there was a certain pallor, a grayness caught from many a vigil.

senses: Someone or something that evolves.
ety: From evolve + -er.
examples: This animal may be a fast runner, but it has been a dreadfully slow evolver.

senses: One who takes part in cosplay.
ety: From Japanese コスプレイヤー (kosupureiyā). Equivalent to cos- + player or cosplay + -er.
examples: The environments and spaces created for and by cosplay provide cosplayers with a variety of spaces for social interactions.

senses: A bird-headed mythological creature and symbol of protection in Māori mythology.
ety: Borrowed from Māori manaia.

senses: A rare blue variety of pectolite found only in the Dominican Republic.
ety: Combination of Larissa and Spanish mar (“sea”). Coined by Miguel Méndez after his 1974 rediscovery of the stone in the Dominican Republic. Named for his daughter Larissa and the Caribbean sea, which has a similar blue color.
